strengths: Novel behavioral perspective on synthetic image detection: the shift from appearance-based to behavior-based detection through robustness asymmetry is well-motivated, intuitive, and clearly demonstrated across multiple foundation models
Strong empirical results: 93.47% average accuracy vs. 85.66% for strongest baseline (7.81% improvement) across comprehensive evaluation of 16 diverse generators and 10+ competing methods

Solid theoretical contribution: Theorem 4.3 establishes rigorous lower bound connecting robustness asymmetry to memorization (SIDE divergence), with Lemma 4.2 grounding the tangent/normal anisotropy assumption in established encoder literature and empirical validation in Appendix B.2

Rigorous experimental protocol: training on single generator (ProGAN) with evaluation on 15 unseen models following established PatchCraft benchmark; thorough ablations (Table 2) quantifying each component contribution; robustness testing under JPEG compression and Gaussian blur

Practical and generalizable design: data- and model-agnostic approach works across different foundation models (DINOv3, CLIP); multi-branch architecture thoughtfully integrates complementary semantic, discrepancy, and low-level evidence; code promised for release

Clear presentation and comprehensive evaluation: well-structured paper with effective visualizations (especially Figures 1, 3); extensive appendices including theoretical proofs and empirical validation; detailed implementation details provided
weaknesses: Insufficient justification for key architectural choices: DRP module uses UNet but no comparison to simpler alternatives (e.g., learned Gaussian noise); Diagonal-Restricted Covariance (DCA) introduced as optional but necessity unclear since embedding distance d already captures shift magnitude; median filtering choice appears empirically driven (Res: Med→Gau ablation shows 90.58% vs 93.47%) without principled justification; margin γ=0.1 lacks sensitivity analysis

Potential circularity in training setup: paper explicitly disables JPEG compression and blur augmentations to ensure 'robustness asymmetry arises solely from the probing module,' yet Appendix A critiques DIRE for exploiting similar dataset biases. Risk that RA-Det performance partially reflects this artificial advantage rather than fundamental asymmetry

Limited generalization analysis: all experiments at 224×224 or 256×256 resolution—unclear if method scales to modern generators using 512×512 or higher; primarily facial images with limited semantic diversity ('other categories' not specified); post-processing robustness (resizing, cropping, user edits) not evaluated

Loose theoretical bounds: lower bound in Theorem 4.3 involves term √M(D; pθ, ε₀) which can be large, weakening guarantee; 'sufficiently small ε' regime never formally defined for practical detection; empirical validation uses training epochs as proxy for SIDE divergence, acknowledged as computationally expensive and loose proxy

Reproducibility gaps: DRP UNet architecture details missing (layer counts, attention specifications, parameter count); validation procedure unclear (separate validation set? model selection criterion?); hyperparameter choices (learning rate 1e-5, batch size 32) unjustified; only 10 training epochs mentioned without convergence verification; computational cost vs. baselines not reported

Incomplete failure mode analysis: 'whichfaceisreal' (72.20% ACC) and Midjourney (80.04% ACC) show notably lower performance without explanation; no visualization of failure cases or learned perturbations; RIGID baseline (most similar behavior-based approach) dismissed quickly despite dramatic improvement (77.17%→93.47%), deserving deeper mechanistic analysis

Missing critical ablations and analyses: no sensitivity studies for perturbation magnitude ε, margin γ, or batch size; no direct comparison between learned vs. fixed perturbations; no evaluation of method robustness against adversarial perturbations designed to fool the detector; batch-level statistics in contrastive loss (Eq. 8) may vary with batch composition

strengths: Novel perspective shifting from appearance-based to behavior-based detection via robustness asymmetry; well-motivated and convincingly demonstrated across multiple foundation models

Strong empirical results: 7.81% improvement over FerretNet (93.47% vs 85.66% accuracy), with consistent performance across 16 diverse generative models spanning GANs, diffusion models, and platform generators
Theoretical contribution providing lower bound (Theorem 4.3) connecting robustness asymmetry to memorization via SIDE divergence, with empirical validation including AMS-based regression analysis

Comprehensive experimental evaluation including multiple training protocols (Table 2), thorough ablations (Table 3), robustness testing under JPEG/blur, and effective cross-generator visualization via radar charts
Demonstrates robustness to common post-processing operations and maintains strong performance across training-source variations, supporting generalization claims
weaknesses: Significant theory-practice gap: theoretical analysis assumes small isotropic perturbations but method uses learned structured perturbations from conditional UNet; lower bound may be loose as it includes term B√(M/2) that grows with weak memorization

Substantial unexplained performance variance across generators (72.20-99.98%, Table 1); limited failure mode analysis and insufficient investigation of why certain generators (e.g., whichfaceisreal, Midjourney) show degraded performance

Design choices lack sufficient justification: (1) conditional UNet architecture for DRP with no architecture ablation, (2) why hand-crafted perturbations fail—insufficient vs. generator-specific information?, (3) median vs. Gaussian filtering choice based on marginal difference (90.58% vs 90.34%)
Computational overhead of 52% (25.14ms vs 16.49ms for UniFD) due to second forward pass and DRP module requires second foundation model pass; impact on deployment scenarios underexplored

Claims of 'universality' overstated: method tested on only 16 models with performance range 72-99%; unclear generalization to different foundation architectures beyond DINOv3/CLIP; no evaluation on cutting-edge generators (DALL-E 3, Gemini, etc.)

Unresolved theory-practice connections: Assumption 4.1 on manifold structure/encoder anisotropy is unverified; empirical validation in Appendix D uses training epochs as indirect memorization proxy (moderate R² of 0.59-0.73 with AMS metric)

Potential dataset format/resolution biases: all experiments use center-cropped 224×224 images; single-generator training protocol (ProGAN) may not reflect real-world mixed distributions; performance drops modestly with SDv1.4-only training

Missing technical details: branch fusion mechanism unspecified (concatenation + MLPs?), contrastive loss motivation not compared to standard sample-level formulations, no analysis of adaptive attacks targeting robustness properties
